clue.text: Don't speak well of French mistress in feature

indicators.note: the French title is placed inside the word meaning feature, which then wraps around it

blocks.note: the star is the featured attraction of a show
Mme is the abbreviation of Madame, the French title for a married woman

explanation.surface: A plea not to gossip about the French mistress who appears in some feature article.
explanation.definitionFit: To stammer is to falter and repeat sounds, failing to talk fluently, so it is not speaking well.

clue.text: Like to go round old city for enjoyment

indicators.note: going round something means encircling it, so one word wraps the other

blocks.note: to please is to like, as in 'do as you please'
Ur is the ancient Sumerian city, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: Someone likes to tour an ancient city simply because they enjoy it.
explanation.definitionFit: Pleasure and enjoyment are direct synonyms, both naming the feeling of happy satisfaction.

clue.text: Trouble on board is frightening

definitions.note: SCARES is the plain present tense, matching 'is frightening' in sense

indicators.note: being on a ship means being aboard it, so the word for trouble goes inside the vessel

blocks.note: care is worry or trouble
SS, steamship, is the ship that 'board' stands for in crosswords

explanation.surface: Some trouble aboard ship is alarming the passengers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On board' conventionally means placed inside SS, the steamship abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To scare someone is to frighten them, so the verb form fits the clue's present continuous phrase.

clue.text: Always reverses broken lead as shown

indicators.note: reverses says the word for always is read from its end back to its start
something broken is smashed apart, so its letters are put back in a different order

blocks.note: ever means always, as in 'for ever'
taken as written, for rearranging

explanation.surface: Someone who always backs away from a broken lead, as demonstrated.
explanation.definitionFit: Something revealed has been exposed or displayed, so it has been shown.

clue.text: Fool is standing in one Italian town

blocks.note: an ass is a fool
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A clown is deputising for someone in an Italian town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing in' just puts the pieces side by side here; it is not asking for anything to go inside anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Assisi is a hill town in Umbria, central Italy, famous as the birthplace of Saint Francis.

clue.text: Busy when given a ring?

blocks.note: first meaning: occupied, as a telephone line is
second meaning: pledged to marry, wearing the ring that seals it

explanation.walkthrough: A ring sounds like a phone call, which would fit busy; it is really the ring a fiancée receives.
explanation.definitionFit: A phone line in use is said to be occupied, and a couple promised to wed have exchanged that pledge.

clue.text: Type inclined to emphasise things

definitions.note: a purpose phrase standing for the noun: what is used to stress words

blocks.note: first meaning: printing type whose letters slope to the right
second meaning: the device writers use to give words stress

explanation.walkthrough: 'Type inclined' reads as a kind of person with a tendency; really it is sloping printing type.
explanation.definitionFit: Italic letters slope to the right and are the standard printed way to give a word stress.

clue.text: Stopping by sea, say, and relaxing

indicators.note: say tells us to use the letter that is pronounced like the word sea

blocks.note: the letter C is pronounced exactly like sea
easing off is relaxing

explanation.surface: Pausing beside the sea to unwind.
explanation.definitionFit: Ceasing means coming to an end or halting, which is what stopping is.

clue.text: Struggle if led off after fighting here

indicators.note: off means gone wrong, so these letters come out in a spoilt order
after places the rearranged letters behind the word for struggle

blocks.note: a battle is a struggle
taken as written, for rearranging

explanation.surface: A struggle breaks out if the leader goes off after the fighting has happened here.
explanation.definitionFit: A battlefield is the ground where armies clash, the place where combat happens.

clue.text: Spoil crossword compiler with male twins

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself as I
M is the abbreviation for male
twins make a pair

explanation.surface: The setter, accompanied by twin boys, ruins things.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords the compiler or setter is often I or ME.
explanation.definitionFit: To impair something is to damage or weaken it, which is to spoil it.

clue.text: Person in a state?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who is agitated or upset
setter's reading: a citizen of one of the United States

explanation.walkthrough: 'In a state' is British slang for flustered; here a state is one of the fifty that make up the USA.
explanation.definitionFit: A citizen of the USA lives in one of its member states, so is literally someone in a state.

clue.text: May be ordered off for scoffing

definitions.text: May be ordered off for scoffing

blocks.clueFragment: May be ordered off for scoffing
blocks.note: surface reading: someone sent away, as from a pitch, for jeering
setter's reading: the list from which diners choose food to eat

explanation.walkthrough: Scoffing means mocking, but also, in British slang, eating greedily; a restaurant list is what you order dishes from.
explanation.definitionFit: A restaurant's list of dishes is what customers choose their meal from when ordering food.

clue.text: Spots a count amongst the space travellers

indicators.note: amongst means surrounded by, so these words sit inside the other word

blocks.note: spots are places, or sites
A plus TELL, an old word for count, as in 'all told'

explanation.surface: Someone spots an astronomical count among the astronauts.
explanation.walkthrough: Tell meaning count survives in tellers who count votes or money.
explanation.definitionFit: Satellites orbit the earth or other bodies, so they are objects that journey through outer space.

clue.text: Dislike taking piano on loan, but it's brilliant!

indicators.note: taking means holding something in, so the word for dislike surrounds the rest

blocks.note: to resent is to dislike bitterly
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
to lend is to give something on loan

explanation.surface: Someone hates having a borrowed piano, though the instrument is splendid.
explanation.definitionFit: Resplendent means dazzlingly bright or splendid in appearance, close in sense to brilliant.

clue.text: The elderly stand in groups - they stop people getting in

indicators.note: in a down clue, standing up means the word is read from bottom to top
in puts the turned word inside the word for groups

blocks.note: the old are the elderly
packs are groups, as of wolves or cards

explanation.surface: Old people stand around in clusters, blocking the way in.
explanation.definitionFit: Padlocks are detachable locks fastened on doors and gates to keep intruders out.

clue.text: Raised article on about staff of emperor

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising a word lifts it so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: an is the indefinite article
a staff is a pole
taken as written

explanation.surface: An item about an emperor's staff officers is published.
explanation.walkthrough: The last word of the wordplay is simply taken literally and tacked on at the end; 'about' is only a joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon Bonaparte crowned himself Emperor of the French in 1804, the most famous holder of that title.

clue.text: Coward speaking of what he did when frightened?

indicators.note: speaking means we take how the name sounds when said, not how it is spelt

blocks.note: the playwright Noël Coward's surname, said aloud

explanation.surface: A tale about the playwright Coward recounting his behaviour when scared.
explanation.walkthrough: Noël Coward was an English playwright; his name in a non-rhotic accent sounds like the past tense of cower.
explanation.definitionFit: To cower is to crouch or shrink back in fear, exactly what a coward does when afraid.

clue.text: Vicar takes tongue back

blocks.note: Rev, Reverend, is a vicar's title
Erse is the Gaelic language of Scotland or Ireland

explanation.surface: A clergyman retracts what he said.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like a reversal signal but it is the definition, as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To back a car is to drive it in reverse, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Because at an auction it's grim?

blocks.note: for can mean because, as in 'for he was tired'
bidding is the offering of prices at an auction

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about why an auction feels so bleak.
explanation.definitionFit: Forbidding describes something stern or threatening in appearance, so unfriendly and grim.

clue.text: Reserved yet finding love good in bed!

indicators.note: in places the words for love and good inside the word for bed

blocks.note: taken as written
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
OK means good, all right

explanation.surface: A shy person nonetheless discovers that romance in bed is good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reserved' looks like it means shy, but it is the definition in its sense of booked ahead.
explanation.definitionFit: A booked table or room has been reserved, set aside in advance for someone.

clue.text: The boss found two fellows in a terrible rage

indicators.note: terrible suggests something messed up, so the letters following are jumbled
in a puts the fellows inside the rearranged word

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow, so two give FF
taken as written, for rearranging

explanation.surface: The manager discovered two men in a furious temper.
explanation.walkthrough: Gaffer is British slang for a boss or foreman.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaffer is informal British for the person in charge, such as a foreman or football manager.

clue.text: Look both ways

indicators.note: both ways means the answer reads the same forwards and backwards

blocks.note: a quick look

explanation.surface: Advice to check left and right, as when crossing a road.
explanation.definitionFit: A peep is a brief or furtive glance, so it is a kind of look.

clue.text: It's designed for lifting a bearing for withdrawing lubricant

indicators.note: withdrawing means pulling back, so this word is read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
E, east, is a compass bearing
taken as written
oil is a lubricant

explanation.surface: A machine part is designed to lift a bearing so lubricant can be drained.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' looks like part of the definition, but it is the word that turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: An aerofoil, such as a wing, is shaped so that air flowing over it produces upward lift.

clue.text: Killed everyone in flat

indicators.note: in puts the word for everyone inside the word for flat

blocks.note: a fen is flat marshy land
all means everyone

explanation.surface: A murder of every occupant in an apartment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' looks like an apartment; it is fenland, the low wet country of eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: The fallen are soldiers killed in battle, so fallen is used to mean slain.

clue.text: Black sweetheart packs ornaments

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter, and the word is fused with its own heart here, so only that centre is kept

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
the middle letter of sweet; 'heart' signals the centre
packs of cards are decks

explanation.surface: A dark-haired lover packs away some decorations.
explanation.definitionFit: To bedeck is to decorate or adorn, so bedecks means ornaments used as a verb.

clue.text: Pity about Rome's redevelopment

indicators.note: redevelopment means rebuilding, so the letters are reconstructed in a new order

blocks.note: re means about, concerning
taken as written, for rearranging

explanation.surface: A lament over the rebuilding of Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pity' is used in its older sense of regret or compunction.
explanation.definitionFit: Remorse is deep regret, and in older usage it also meant compassion, close to pity.
